summary.title: A Distributed Systems Reading List
summary.one_liner: A quick-reference primer on distributed systems theory (system models, failure modes, consensus, FLP, CAP, consistency models, logical clocks, CRDTs) with pointers to foundational papers and books.
takeaways: Distributed system models (synchronous, semi-synchronous, asynchronous) and failure modes (crash, omission, performance, Byzantine) define what guarantees are possible.

FLP shows consensus is unsolvable in a purely asynchronous model with any possible failure; CAP forces a choice between availability and consistency under partitions, refined by PACELC and yield/harvest.
Message delivery semantics, ordering (total, partial, causal), and idempotence determine how replicated systems behave under retries and reordering.
Common practical faults include netsplits, split brain, timeouts, clock drift, and missing messages from ordering; clients are part of the system too.
Consistency models, logical clocks, and CRDTs provide tools for reasoning about ordering and conflicts, and the Kleppmann book is recommended as a single consolidated source.
summary.summary: The page is a personal reference written by the author in 2019 for coworkers and republished on the blog, with links re-verified and some replaced by archive links. It walks through distributed systems theory in short sections: system models, failure modes, consensus and the FLP result, fault detection, CAP theorem and its refinements, message-passing and ordering definitions, idempotence, replication approaches, end-to-end arguments, practical failure modes, consistency models, logical clocks, and CRDTs. Each section gives brief definitions and points to papers and talks (such as Raft, Paxos, ZAB, and the Dynamo paper) for deeper reading. It closes with a recommendation of Designing Data-Intensive Applications by Martin Kleppmann.
